entry.title: Was Napoleon Betrayed? The Events Surrounding his First Abdication

media:group.media:title: Was Napoleon Betrayed? The Events Surrounding his First Abdication
media:group.media:description:
In March 1814, the capture of Paris by the Allies triggered a series of events that led to Napoleon’s unconditional abdication. However, for a time it seemed possible that although Napoleon would not be able to save the throne for himself, he might have been able to do so for his son and heir. This was not to be, but was this because of traitors, or were the events merely the result of Napoleon’s own mistakes? In this video we will discuss the events surrounding the fall of Paris, along with the events that led to Napoleon facing exile on the island of Elba.

entry.title: Failure at Wagram: Bernadotte's Blunders during the 1809 Campaign

media:group.media:title: Failure at Wagram: Bernadotte's Blunders during the 1809 Campaign
media:group.media:description:
Marshal Bernadotte is a divisive figure and although his performance during the 1806 Campaign is often criticised, particularly due to his absence at the twin battles of Jena and Auerstadt, his behaviour during the 1809 Campaign, and in particular at the battle of Wagram, often goes under the radar. This is strange because the campaign would end for Bernadotte with his removal from the army, supposedly for his poor performance during the battle. It should then prove perfect fuel for his many critics, yet often it is overlooked. Therefore, in the following video, we shall examine his actions during this campaign on the Danube and discover why exactly he was fired, before discussing whether or not it was justified.

entry.title: Bernadotte and Napoleon: Friends or Enemies?

media:group.media:title: Bernadotte and Napoleon: Friends or Enemies?
media:group.media:description:
The relationship between Bernadotte and Napoleon is often shaded by later events, namely Bernadotte's supposed defection in joining the Coalition Forces against France. This has unfortunately led many people to conclude that the two men had therefore always shared a mutual contempt and were enemies from the start. The truth, however, is more complicated, and in this video we track their relationship from their first meeting in 1797 until 1809, the point at which a divide does truly begin to appear.

entry.title: The Bernadotte Controversy -The Case of the Missing Marshal, 1806

media:group.media:title: The Bernadotte Controversy -The Case of the Missing Marshal, 1806
media:group.media:description:
The Campaign of 1806 in Saxony saw Napoleon and the French crush the Prussian armies, with the focal point being the twin battles of Jena and Auerstadt on the 14th October. Both were French victories, though at Auerstadt Marshal Davout had been forced to face the majority of the Prussian army entirely alone. The blame for this has frequently been laid at the feet of Marshal Bernadotte who, despite his corps spending the day within marching distance of both battles, took no active part in either engagement. Bernadotte always maintained his innocence and stated that his actions were guided by his orders, but many writers since then have called his behavior into question and have even suggested treachery. In the following video we will attempt to discern the truth of the situation, find out what exactly happened on the 14th October, and try and figure out why, before determining who was ultimately to blame.

entry.title: The Genius of the Corps System - Napoleon and the Campaign of 1806

media:group.media:title: The Genius of the Corps System - Napoleon and the Campaign of 1806
media:group.media:description:
The army corps system, perfected by the French under Napoleon, was revolutionary in the flexibility with which it provided an army commander. Each corps, acting as a self contained element, could be used in a variety of ways, both on and off the battlefield. In this video I analyse how this system functioned under Napoleon, and use the Campaign of Jena in 1806 as an example to illustrate its brilliance.

entry.title: Moving Armies: The Logistical System of Napoleon's Grande Armée

media:group.media:title: Moving Armies: The Logistical System of Napoleon's Grande Armée
media:group.media:description:
The great strategic manoeuvres of Ulm and Jena conducted by the Grand Armée are often credited to the genius of Napoleon. Whilst their creation was no doubt impressive, it was frequently the sheer speed at which these manoeuvres were carried out that propelled them to such success. The key to these operational speeds can be seen in several places, but one of the most important was the logistical system by which the French army operated. In the following video we will discuss how this system worked, and explain how it enabled la Grande Armée to dominate the armies of the Old Order.

entry.title: Victors Write the History: A discussion into the assessment of battles in the age of Napoleon

media:group.media:title: Victors Write the History: A discussion into the assessment of battles in the age of Napoleon
media:group.media:description:
Who won the battle? A simple question, yet too frequently in military history one can find different answers to that question depending upon the writer. The reasons for this variation are at times genuine but unfortunately sometimes they are not. Whatever the reason, this does then raise the questions; how exactly do we analyse the outcome of encounters? and what exactly is it that we place the most value on when assigning victory or defeat? Both valid questions, and therefore in the following video I am going to attempt to answer them, pulling apart what I deem to be the most common methods of analysis, discussing the method that I currently use, before then offering my thoughts over several Napoleonic battles that frequently sport different results.

media:group.media:title: The Tactics and Strategy of Napoleon - Building la Grande Armée Part IV: Grand Tactics and Strategy
media:group.media:description:
Napoleon is regularly regarded as a military genius, on par with the likes of Alexander, Caesar, and Frederick the Great, but was this really the case? The previous three videos in this series have already shown how far the three individual arms of la Grande Armée were ahead of their rivals, and once established under the corps system, they offered Napoleon a deadly weapon not entirely of his own making. Was his success therefore inevitable or was he in fact a true master of war? In the following video we look into the development on the corps system before discussing the tactics and strategies used by the French and Napoleon during this period of dominance.

entry.title: Napoleon's Artillery and their Tactics - Building la Grande Armée Part III

media:group.media:title: Napoleon's Artillery and their Tactics - Building la Grande Armée Part III
media:group.media:description:
The Napoleonic Wars were perhaps the first artillery wars, the place where the arm truly became formidable and independent, and it was the French that forged the way in this regard. Although led by one of the greatest gunners of the age, the dominance that they would show in this realm cannot be totally credited to Napoleon. Whilst he may have put the final pieces in place, the solid foundations had been laid much earlier, and glimpses of success showed before he ever took charge in the field. In the following video I will examine this growth, highlighting the key markers that set the stage for la Grand Armée’s artillerymen to dominate European battlefields.

entry.title: Why Didn't Napoleon Use Observation Balloons?

media:group.media:title: Why Didn't Napoleon Use Observation Balloons?
media:group.media:description:
Despite Observation Balloons being readily available throughout the period, why did neither Napoleon, nor any of his rivals, take advantage of such technology? In the following video I will give an overview of the early development of both the Hot air and Hydrogen balloons, their use during the French Revolutionary Wars, and ultimately offer my conclusions as to why I believe they played no major part in the Napoleonic Wars that followed.

entry.title: Napoleon's Cavalry and their Tactics - Building la Grande Armée: Part II

media:group.media:title: Napoleon's Cavalry and their Tactics - Building la Grande Armée: Part II
media:group.media:description:
Led by such enigmatic characters as Murat, Lasalle, d’Hautpoul, and Kellerman, the French cavalry became the most potent in all of Europe during the first decade of the 19th century. However, neglect by previous regimes meant that they boasted a mediocre record during the Revolutionary Wars, and it wasn’t until the time of the Empire that they truly reached their peak. In the following video we track this development, discuss their tactics, and figure out how they became so dominant, rightly earning their spot as part of Napoleon’s most potent weapon, la Grande Armée.

entry.title: Napoleon's Infantry and their Tactics - Building la Grande Armée: Part I

media:group.media:title: Napoleon's Infantry and their Tactics - Building la Grande Armée: Part I
media:group.media:description:
Napoleon's rampage across Europe from 1805-1807, not only humbled the Old Regimes, but it was also the signal for a completely new style of warfare. This style was not of the Emperor's making, instead owing its origins to military minds of the previous century, however it did come to a peak under his leadership.
In part one of this series I delve into the tactics that set the infantry of la Grande Armée above its peers, discussing their origins, and how a culmination of events led to an ushering in of this new French style of warfare.
